The crunch spread is not: Token Price - GPU rental price. 

Rather it is: (Token Price * Token Volume) - GPU rental price.

More simply: Revenue per GPU - GPU rental price.

Continuous throughput improvements for the same exact token mean that volume growth can more than offset token price declines for the exact same model/token

i.e. Kimi K3 token throughput per GPU has recently been improving at a 37% annualized rate driven by inference engine optimizations.

GPU prices are vertical because:

1) Mix is shifting from higher margin frontier tokens to lower margin open-weight tokens. $10 in Claude revenue requires $1 of inference compute. $10 of of open-weight revenue requires $3 to $7 of inference compute given competition between inference providers leads to lower margins. Open-weight tokens taking share is positive for AI infrastructure demand given lower margins at the model layer. The reverse is also true in that frontier tokens taking share is negative for AI infrastructure demand. Open-weight models have been taking share since early summer.

2) Throughput is steadily improving for each individual token type such that GPU compute becomes more valuable even as true like for like token prices decline.

As noted in the article from @C_Barraud, investors were bracing for Moody's ratings review on French debt, but the country got some relief after a brutal week which saw the 10-year yield hitting 5% for the first time since 2002, and widening the most against German yields in records dating to 1990.

Heading into Friday most economists expected Moody's to cut France one notch, from Aa3 to A1.  

But it didn't. Instead, Moody's took no rating action, leaving France at Aa3 with a negative outlook. It said this wasn't a credit action and seems to be waiting for more clarity on the budget. It also said higher borrowing costs would need to persist for an extended period to seriously hurt debt sustainability.

The longer view though is sobering. France held AAA ratings from all three major agencies until 2012. Since then it has received 11 downgrades: four from S&P, four from Fitch and three from Moody's. S&P and Fitch now rate France A+, which leaves Moody's as the last of the big three still rating France in the AA tier. 

The negative outlook keeps a downgrade on the table, and S&P reviews France again on Nov 27.

Yes, I like $SIVE. It's a fun company to cover, since there's a lot of supply chain alpha here. 

But the company completely Tall Poppy Syndromed itself last earnings. 

And it's clearly shown in the drawdown. 

Bit of a longer consolidated thought and some scattered bits of supply chain info: 

- Sivers has 100M CW DFB laser capacity coming online Q4 2027 during an industry shortage. 

And very large allocations from foundries online (they were doing these quals with Win Semi + 2 others back in 2023/2024), so they can actively monetize the bottleneck today. 

The other interesting reason why bottlenecks are important (aside from ASP hikes), is because qualifications convert much faster + more likely given incentives around supply scarcity.

-> As one example, module makers have expanded the amount of suppliers, eg. (lightcounting cited companies expanding to 5-7+ suppliers from 2-3). 

Innolight, for example last month responded to a question addressing tight 1.6T DFB laser supply in 2026–2027:

- Innolight was actively introducing new suppliers last month and are planning to sign 2-3 year-long contracts to lock upstream capacity

-> This is while your biggest merchant laser companies making up the world's 600m+ EML/CW laser capacity like $COHR have redirected lasers to their own programs. $LITE sold out into 2029, Landmark also locked a lot of their capacity into 2027-2029. $AAOI was an expected player, but ended up redirecting lasers into their own transceiver programs too. 

And this coincides with times $SIVE has tremendous capacity available now + actively engaged with Chinese pluggables players (not saying it's Innolight, but just shows Chinese makers like Cambridge/Eoptolink are actively trying to secure laser capacity). 

- Fun to note, before $JBL was announced, Sivers had and has ongoing direct engagements with hyperscalers as well. 

We saw that hyperscalers approached $MTSI and $AAOI for laser capacity from their earnings transcripts (and hilariously got turned away from AAOI due to shortages).

So the odds pluggable makers or hyperscalers end up converting to capacity agreements with $SIVE seems a materially higher. 

Just a little rant: for all the sellside/retail trying to model revenue, you can't just slap on a stupid 25-35% CAGR on NRE revenue since it's close to 0 revenue now.

Especially when they scale up to maybe 300M laser capacity (extrapolated from 2:1 external/internal capacity).

It's also not the same as $POET having OE packaging capacity at scale, since lasers are in a genuine shortage. So capacity is more likely to convert like how $AAOI is sold out, $LITE is sold out into 2029  

We've already seen what revenue that laser capacity brings in since $LITE cited $5B in laser capacity from just one 2028 fab alone in Greensboro (on higher end ranges). 

And whatever lasers Sivers sell, they're targeting ~50-60+ blended gross margins long term on maybe $3-6 for lower range lasers to $6-$12 for high end custom deployments. But no disclosures around capacity -> revenue conversion yet from Sivers.

Now here's the thing people don't really understand, "why no revenue?" for current opportunities? 

$SIVE pre 2024 focused on custom development for future architectural shifts like CPO. 

For custom deployments:  

- We finally got conversion from 1 of their 4 or so lidar customers this week with ~ $AEVA. 
- ~ $APPL was confirmed ongoing earlier this year with an explanation that "It takes tremendous amount of trials and algorithms way beyond just what we supply to them". 
- All their customers from 2023-2024 like Ayar and 3 others, probably achieve volume in 2028 as CPO takes off. 

Custom high end lasers programs are extremely sticky but take many years and are mainly NRE. And as seen with CPO scale up, faced delays with commercialization over the years.

1/ On Squiggle #6529
 
I would like to explain why we are excited about “buying a Squiggle” 
 
While Squiggles are, in fact, sweet, the exciting part is that every part of this process happened in a decentralized manner.
 
2/ @aRegularDad proposed a Meme Card to fund a Squiggle acquisition.

81 profiles participated in the Main Stage vote and voted with TDH to mint this as a Meme Card

The card won. 77 paid editions were minted, providing 2.51 ETH for the acquisition.
 
3/  @cheesebiz  and @bankons helped scout and connected @squiggleDAO . SquiggleDAO suggested trying to acquire Squiggle 6529
 
The price was 3.01 ETH, so @MadaCollects who had been following the discussion, chipped in another 0.5 ETH to the pool (respect!)
 
4/ The seller wanted to stay anonymous, preserve the provenance (no intermediary transfers) and keep their vault secure.

Ultimately, the seller trusted SquiggleDAO and 6529 network and sent the Squiggle directly to the 6529 Network Museum before receiving payment.

5/ Reminder: What is the 6529 network museum? It is a SAFE vault organized by TDH, owned by the network, a cultural asset, NFTs go in, but ~they do not go out. 
 
It is the network-native concept of a national public museum
 
6/ Finally, one more step to replace the temporary art on the card with something appropriate for the long-term. Well, another TDH vote of course.
 
@ricardotakamura  won with THE VAULT, a long-exposure light painting made at Casa NUA in Brazil.
 
7/ So to recap:
- Decentralized network mints a meme card to buy a squiggle
- Decentralized network picks which squiggle to buy
- Decentralized network updates the art
- Decentralized network permanent home for the squiggle
 
8/ What was my contribution to any step of this project? 

Nothing at all. I was not involved at all in any way. 

I had a vague awareness that it was happening, but was not following any of the details, let alone helping.
 
9/ Now, some of you are thinking “ok, fine, that is cute, the NFT nerds are collecting NFTs again”
 
Maybe. 
 
Or maybe collecting NFTs is a generalizable proof of concept, and there is no actual limit to this primitive.
 
We will see soon enough.
 
10/ Thank you to all who organized, the voters and everyone who minted.
 
Great job by all.

“If you're providing social services to an immigrant population, then that's not necessarily a productive immigrant population in terms of being able to contribute to growing the economy and supporting civil society.

But if a population of immigrants come in and they're productive, meaning they can get jobs and they can work, and they can support themselves, that means they're adding something positive to the economy, to the civil society, and that is the sort of selection criteria that needs to take place.

If you put the patch there, it's a virtual patch, so any attacker trying to access that vulnerability gets stopped at the perimeter because we know what they're looking for.

Guess what? The phones keep ringing every day, and the conversation always is, ‘Now how do I get out of this? Because I'm tired of getting punched in the face every morning when I wake up.’”

Drawdowns are the norm. New highs are the exception.

This view is a bit too binary. 

There are many problems that don’t require one to be a user of the system — like consensus or improving snarks. That’s OK since they are core comp sci problems. 

However, the main issue today, is that many problems facing Ethereum are user experience issues caused by the platform itself. 

If the core developers are not using the platform — from an actual usage or building on top of perspective — then they cant properly prioritise the issues that need to be fixed. 

This is why there was so misplaced hype around long term strawman proposals vs fixing low hanging fruit (like sponsored transactions or increasing gas limits) that would immediately help users.

Core Developers, EF, everyone involved needs to treat Ethereum the network as a product and not an ideological-driven machine.
